sections.html:
Laurens County sits in the Upstate, inside the Greenville-Anderson-Greer metro area. The city of Laurens serves as the seat and the largest community, and Clinton is the second main town. The 2020 census found 67,539 residents, with about 64 percent in rural areas.

A farmhouse outside Gray Court and a bungalow in town are taxed by the same offices yet attract different buyers. Older housing is common, from mill-era houses to farm property handed down through generations. An inherited house tends to come with an unpaid tax bill, a muddy title or no occupant, and any of these can hold up a closing.

Property tax runs through four county offices, and each answers a different question.

  • Assessor, 864-984-6546: appraises real property and answers legal residence questions.
  • Auditor, 864-984-2535: figures the tax and processes exemption paperwork.
  • Treasurer: takes payments, but neither sets amounts nor keeps owner records.
  • Tax Collector, 864-984-4742: handles accounts still unpaid after the March deadline.

Because the Treasurer holds no owner records, a bill sent to a stale address can go astray. After inheriting or buying a house, notify the Assessor of your address. Rate increases originate with County Council, the school board and municipal councils, which set their own revenue needs, and not with the Treasurer.

Pay by January 15 and no penalty applies. A weekend or holiday on that date extends the deadline to 5:00 p.m. the next business day, and the county must mail bills 30 or more days in advance.

DateWhat happens
January 15Last day to pay without penalty
January 16 onward3 percent penalty (S.C. Code 12-45-180)
February 27 percent more
March 16Unpaid accounts handed to the Tax Collector
March 175 percent more, and the Treasurer may issue a tax execution

Together they add 15 percent to a bill left until March, before any collection costs. Many troubled accounts on inherited houses began with a bill nobody opened in January.

Write to the Assessor within 90 days of the day the notice went out. You can dispute fair market value, special use value or the assessment ratio.

State law requires a written notice in just two situations, when the Assessor raises a value by $1,000 or more and when a property is assessed for the first time. If none reached you, you may appeal in writing at any time. Filing ahead of the first penalty date applies the appeal to the current tax year, and filing on or after it applies to the next.

The Assessor, 864-984-6546, can give you the form and explain the next step. Before you withhold any payment, ask which balance stays protected while an appeal is open.

Two assessment ratios matter on a Laurens County house. Your own home can be taxed on 4 percent of fair market value if it qualifies as a legal residence. Everything else is taxed on 6 percent, which makes a non-qualifying house one and a half times as costly per dollar of value.

The legal residence ratio comes with strings, found in S.C. Code 12-43-220:

  • You own the house and live in it.
  • You swear, under penalty of perjury, that nobody in your household claims the ratio on another home.
  • You rent it out no more than 72 days in a calendar year.
  • When you sell, the buyer files a new application and you tell the assessor within six months.

Timing is unforgiving. File before the first penalty date of the first year you claim the ratio. A fall closing where the buyer misses that date leaves the house at 6 percent for the year.

Seniors, owners certified totally and permanently disabled and legally blind owners may also qualify for the county homestead exemption, which excludes the first $50,000 of a legal residence's value. Applications go through the Auditor.

The Delinquent Tax Collector's office conducts the sale under Chapter 51 of Title 12. After it, the owner keeps a twelve-month right to redeem.

The sale list is published in the Laurens County Advertiser and the Clinton Chronicle. The Forfeited Land Commission gets the opening bid, and bidders must register beforehand and attend in person. A tax deed follows within 45 days once the redemption period ends. Because sale dates change yearly, call 864-984-4742 for the current one.

Interest owed on redemption, set by S.C. Code 12-51-90, is a percentage of the bid that grows each quarter: 3 percent for months 1 to 3, 6 percent for months 4 to 6, 9 percent for months 7 to 9 and 12 percent for months 10 to 12. Those who may redeem are the defaulting owner, the owner's grantee, and a mortgage or judgment creditor.

Closing day is when the year's tax gets paid. The title company takes any open balance out of what the seller would receive. Since penalties shift on set dates, ask the Treasurer or Tax Collector for the exact payoff shortly before you sign.

Sellers in this county keep running into the same few problems:

  • The bill went to a late parent's address and sat unopened.
  • Penalties started January 16 and kept building through March.
  • The legal residence ratio lapsed after a move, and the 6 percent ratio took over.
  • An aging house needs repairs that a lender would not finance.

Someone with a tax debt or a repair list can sell as-is for cash instead. Escrow clears the tax from the proceeds, so you need no money in advance, and with no lender involved there are no repair demands to meet. You can usually pick the closing date. Ask for any payoff figure in writing first.

When you visit an office, carry your deed, newest bill and ID. If the buyer will get next year's bill, ask the Assessor to update the mailing address on the account.

Inherited property tends to raise the same few questions, and each one has a short answer.

  1. Find the tax bills. Check the old address first, because the Treasurer keeps no owner records and mail may have gone there.
  2. Ask the Assessor to correct the address, and ask whether the legal residence ratio is still on the account or lapsed after the owner moved or died.
  3. Call the Tax Collector if the account is delinquent, and ask whether a sale date has been set.
  4. Gather the estate paperwork so the title company can clear the deed.

Once you have all four answers, you know what is owed, who to pay and how much time you have, so choosing between a listing and an as-is cash sale gets easier.

faqs.q: When are Laurens County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Penalty-free through January 15. When that date is a weekend or holiday, you have until 5:00 p.m. the next business day.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a delinquent Laurens County tax bill?
faqs.a: Call the Tax Collector, 864-984-4742. Past-due accounts move to that office after March 16.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my Laurens County assessment?
faqs.a: Yes, by written objection to the Assessor, filed within 90 days of the notice's mailing date. The form is available at 864-984-6546.

faqs.q: Which Laurens County homes are taxed at 4 percent?
faqs.a: A legal residence only. Everything else is at 6 percent, and renting out the home more than 72 days a year can forfeit the lower ratio.

faqs.q: How long can I redeem a Laurens County house after a tax sale?
faqs.a: Twelve months from the sale date under state law. Interest rises from 3 to 12 percent of the bid, depending on which quarter you redeem in.
